title: HuR Inhibition Attenuates Hypertension and Fibrosis in Chronic Kidney Disease.
abstract: Upregulation of the RNA-binding protein HuR (human antigen R) has been reported in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), but its pathogenic role remains incompletely understood. We hypothesized that HuR promotes renal and vascular injury in hypertensive CKD and that pharmacological inhibition of HuR attenuates disease progression. We therefore investigated the role of HuR in deoxycorticosterone acetate (DOCA) plus Ang II (angiotensin II)-induced CKD and evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of the HuR inhibitor, KH3 . Male mice underwent uninephrectomy followed by DOCA+Ang II infusion with 1% NaCl in drinking water and were treated with KH3 or vehicle for 3 weeks. Control mice received saline without DOCA or Ang II. DOCA+Ang II markedly increased HuR expression in circulating exosomes and kidney tissues, which was attenuated by KH3 treatment. KH3 reduced albuminuria, improved renal function, and attenuated kidney hypertrophy, glomerular, and tubulointerstitial fibrosis. These renoprotective effects were associated with reduced podocyte and tubular injury, decreased macrophage infiltration, and suppression of NF-κB (nuclear factor-kappa B) p65, Nox2 (NADPH oxidase 2), AKT (protein kinase B) phosphorylation, TGFβ1 (transforming growth factor β1), and Wisp1 (WNT1-inducible signaling pathway protein 1) signaling. KH3 also partially lowered arterial blood pressure in DOCA+Ang II-treated mice. Further studies in vascular smooth muscle cells and mesenteric resistance arteries suggested that HuR inhibition may suppress vascular profibrotic signaling associated with SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2). HuR is upregulated in renal and vascular tissues in DOCA+Ang II-induced CKD and contributes to renal inflammation, oxidative stress, fibrosis, and vascular dysfunction. Pharmacological inhibition of HuR attenuates renal and vascular injury, supporting HuR as a promising therapeutic target for CKD.

title: Acute degradation of Pumilio proteins reveals a biphasic posttranscriptional regulatory hierarchy in embryonic stem cell fate decision.
abstract: Posttranscriptional regulation is critical for mammalian embryogenesis yet has been underexplored. We previously showed that RNA-binding Pumilio proteins (Pum1/2) are essential for early mouse embryogenesis and embryonic stem cell (ESC) functions. Here, using acute protein degradation systems combined with time-resolved RNA sequencing and enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation, we delineate a two-phase regulatory hierarchy modulated by Pum1/2 in mouse ESCs. The first phase, occurring within 10 h of Pum1/2 depletion, is predominantly stabilization of over 100 Pum1/2-target mRNAs, while the second phase, occurring in subsequent 66 h, propagates to over 1,000 mRNAs mostly through indirect regulatory effects. Functionally, Pum1/2 depletion delays transition from naïve to formative pluripotency and alters expression trajectories of neuroectoderm and germline genes during early differentiation. Mechanistically, Pum1/2 directly repress mRNAs encoding Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 subunits, including Suz12, thereby potentially constraining H3K27me3 deposition at neuroectodermal gene loci. These findings establish Pum1/2 as biphasic posttranscriptional regulators of pluripotency and lineage balance.
extra: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

title: CRISPR interference-based gene silencing in insects: from functional genomics to prospective insect-pest management applications.
abstract: Insect-pests remain a major constraint to global agriculture, causing yield losses through direct feeding and transmission of phytopathogens. Chemical pesticides and transgenic crops expressing Bacillus thuringiensis toxins have shown initial success; however, their use is increasingly constrained by resistance, non-target effects, environmental contamination and regulatory restrictions. Although RNA interference (RNAi) presents a targeted and eco-friendly alternative, it is limited by species variability, rapid double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) degradation, inconsistent silencing and off-target effects. Nuclease-active Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) enables genetic editing, but its irreversible genome modifications raise ethical, ecological and regulatory concerns. CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) offers a programmable approach for sequence-specific, reversible transcriptional suppression without inducing double-strand DNA breaks. Using catalytically inactive Cas9 (dead Cas9 or dCas9) -guided by single-guide RNA (sgRNA), CRISPRi inhibits transcription initiation or elongation while maintaining genomic integrity. Experimental studies in insect models, including disease-vector mosquitoes, have demonstrated effective suppression of coding and non-coding genes, supporting CRISPRi as a functional genomics tool. This review discusses CRISPRi mechanisms, applications, advantages and limitations in insects, comparing it with RNAi and CRISPR/Cas9. Overall, current evidences indicate that CRISPRi is a precise and non-mutagenic platform for insect-pest management, particularly where controlled, reversible and species-specific gene regulation is desirable. However, its application in agricultural pest management remains an extrapolation from functional-genomics studies and requires validation in pest species under whole-organism and field-relevant conditions.

title: Cerebrovascular mechanisms of stroke severity in offspring from pre-eclamptic pregnancy.
abstract: Offspring from pre-eclamptic pregnancies face elevated ischaemic stroke risk throughout life, yet the mechanisms linking adverse intrauterine exposure to adult cerebrovascular vulnerability remain unknown. Distal leptomeningeal anastomoses (LMAs), which develop during late gestation are key determinants of stroke severity and represent a plausible target of prenatal programming. Here, we show that experimental preeclampsia (ePE) in rats establishes a persistent cerebrovascular structural and transcriptional phenotype in adult offspring. Following transient middle cerebral artery occlusion, ePE-exposed males exhibited increased infarct volume, oedema, enhanced perfusion deficit and smaller LMA diameters relative to normal pregnant offspring, and 83% had microvascular stasis after stroke. Female offspring were protected from stroke-induced brain injury despite sharing a similar transcriptional landscape. RNA sequencing and DNA methylation profiling revealed differentially expressed genes and discrete differentially methylated regions enriched for vascular development and VEGF-Notch signalling in ePE offspring. These findings support the possibility of a developmental origin of cerebrovascular stroke risk, implicating gestational programming of cerebrovascular gene expression as a sex modulated determinant of adult stroke outcome and a potential target for early intervention. KEY POINTS: Offspring born from pre-eclamptic pregnancies have a greater lifetime risk and death from ischaemic stroke, but why this occurs is unknown. Pial collaterals form during the late gestational period and are a key determinant of stroke severity. Using a rat model, we showed that compared to normal pregnancy, male offspring from pre-eclamptic pregnancies had smaller diameter pial collaterals which was associated with decreased collateral recruitment during ischaemic stroke and worsened stroke outcome. RNA analysis revealed altered expression of genes related to blood vessel development and function in adult offspring. These findings suggest that preeclampsia leads to lasting changes in cerebrovascular structure and gene expression which is associated with increased stroke severity in male offspring suggesting a potential window for early intervention.

title: Draft genome sequence of Escherichia coli ECMC01 isolated from clinical bovine mastitis in Malaysia.
abstract: The draft genome sequence of Escherichia coli ECMC01 isolated from bovine mastitis in Malaysia is reported. The 5.13-Mb genome encodes 4,967 predicted protein-coding genes, 92 RNA genes, and multiple determinants associated with antimicrobial resistance and virulence.

title: PCSK9 as a Regulatory Network: Molecular Mechanisms, Therapeutic Targeting, and Herbal Modulation.
abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a central regulator of cholesterol homeostasis through its role in promoting low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) degradation and limiting hepatic low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) clearance. The clinical success of monoclonal antibodies and small interfering RNA (siRNA)-based therapies has established PCSK9 as an important therapeutic target. However, PCSK9 biology extends beyond its canonical role in LDLR degradation, with its expression and activity regulated through interconnected transcriptional, post-transcriptional, metabolic, and intracellular signaling mechanisms involving sterol regulatory element-binding protein-2 (SREBP-2), hepatocyte nuclear factor-1α (HNF-1α), microRNAs, and multiple signaling pathways. This regulatory complexity is illustrated by compensatory responses, including statin-induced PCSK9 expression, and by observations that changes in PCSK9 expression do not always directly predict overall metabolic outcomes. Current therapeutic strategies primarily target circulating PCSK9 or suppress its hepatic synthesis, whereas upstream and multi-level regulatory mechanisms remain less extensively explored. Herbal-derived compounds have emerged as potential multi-target modulators of the PCSK9 regulatory network, with experimental studies indicating that phytochemicals and plant extracts may influence PCSK9 through coordinated effects on transcriptional regulators, cellular signaling pathways, and LDLR expression. Nevertheless, the available evidence is heterogeneous, with substantial variation in experimental models, phytochemical composition, dosing strategies, and mechanistic endpoints. This review integrates current evidence on the molecular regulation of PCSK9, established and emerging therapeutic strategies, and herbal modulation across in vitro, in vivo, and in silico studies. Overall, the evidence supports a network-based interpretation of PCSK9 regulation and suggests that multi-target herbal modulation may provide a complementary strategy to conventional PCSK9-directed therapies by acting at multiple regulatory levels. However, the predominantly preclinical nature of the available evidence underscores the need for standardized phytochemical characterization, rigorous mechanistic validation, and well-designed clinical studies before therapeutic translation can be established.

title: Conserved and taxon-restricted orthogroup expansions of pan-eukaryotic protein complexes.
abstract: Protein complexes are central to cell biology and typically verified via a combination of interaction data, complete genome sequencing and comprehensive protein-coding gene predictions for reference eukaryotes. However, this information is lacking for non-reference eukaryotes. Protein complexes can be predicted in species for which no interaction data is available by mapping orthology of verified protein complex components from reference eukaryotes to predicted proteomes. Studies that map conservation of protein complex components by orthology are often limited to a small number of protein queries, an under-representation of non-reference, microbial eukaryotes and are scattered across the literature. Here, I integrate orthology and protein interaction data by mapping proteins of experimentally verified complexes to orthogroups of proteins spanning 31 diverse eukaryotes. Proteins within complex-harbouring orthogroups are retained and distributed more evenly across taxa than non-complex orthogroups. I identified 184 universal orthogroups that included orthologs of known protein complex components from all 31 eukaryotes, consistent with a conserved core repertoire, likely present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA). I generated the protein complex orthology cartographer (PCOC) suite to find significant duplications and reductions of proteins in universal orthogroups across and between eukaryotes. This revealed both multi-copy and notably single-copy proteins, in all queried species, from the exosome, spliceosome, proteasome, small-ribosomal processome, tRNA synthetases, MCM complexes and RNA polymerase III. Case analyses of Naegleria gruberi and Guillardia theta highlight taxon-specific expansions and show how broader protist inclusion improves domain-wide inference of eukaryotic protein-complex evolution.

title: Allele-selective targeting of uromodulin by antisense oligonucleotides reduces aggregates and kidney damage in a mouse model of autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease.
abstract: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (ADTKD) arises from gain-of-toxic-function mutations in the UMOD gene coding for uromodulin, the most abundant protein excreted in normal urine. Mutant uromodulin accumulates in the cells lining the thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of Henle, leading to intracellular aggregates, cellular stress, and kidney damage. Here, we demonstrate that an antisense gapmer oligonucleotide (ASO) designed against the representative c.553C > A (p.R185S) UMOD mutation produced allele-selective silencing of the mutant messenger RNA and protein in kidney cells. Short-term administration of a murine ASO analogue in the established Umod R186S/+ mouse model of ADTKD suppressed uromodulin and lowered tubular damage, whereas a non-targeting scrambled control was inactive. After a 4-week treatment, ASO accumulation in the Umod R186S/+ kidneys reached ∼320 000 copies per TAL cell, quantified using a sensitive splint-ligation assay. The ASO treatment suppressed premature mutant uromodulin and its toxic aggregates in Umod R186S/+ kidneys, whereas it had no effects on wild-type uromodulin in Umod +/+ kidneys. Notably, the ASO improved tubular function and decreased kidney tubulointerstitial inflammation in Umod R186S/+ mice. This work offers a roadmap for antisense therapy to treat ADTKD-UMOD and substantiates the therapeutic potential of ASOs in disorders of the kidney tubule.

title: UV-induced translation capacity in Fusarium mangiferae.
abstract: In fast-growing cells, most RNA molecules encode ribosomal subunits. During growth arrest caused by DNA damage, ribosome biogenesis decreases because it is highly energy-demanding. This was observed in cells from bacteria, yeast, and humans. Here, we report that in Fusarium mangiferae, UV radiation significantly induces ribosome levels and translation capacity. This UV-induced response occurs after filament formation. Translation induction modestly but significantly enhances both UV survival and repair. While some mRNAs differentially associated with ribosomes after UV exposure are linked to DNA repair, most belong to modules involved in protein folding and gene expression. TOR signaling is required for the immediate UV induction of ribosome biogenesis genes. However, we provide evidence that UV induces mechanisms that operate upstream of, or in parallel with, TOR. These findings suggest a novel type of response to DNA damage, in which the primary aim is to protect gene expression from the detrimental effects of UV radiation on transcription.

title: Non-Canonical Function of DDX21 in Fetal Hematopoiesis Antagonizes KDM5A-Mediated Repression of Ribosomal and Hematopoietic Genes.
abstract: Ribosome biogenesis is crucial for meeting the elevated biosynthetic demands of rapidly expanding fetal hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) during fetal development. Ddx21 is a DEAD-box RNA helicase required for ribosome biogenesis, but its role in fetal hematopoiesis remains undefined. Here, we show that hematopoietic-specific deletion of Ddx21 in mice results in severe fetal anemia, HSPC depletion, and loss of reconstitution capacity. Mechanistically, Ddx21 directly binds the histone demethylase Kdm5a via its helicase D2 domain in an RNA-dependent manner. Ddx21 and Kdm5a co-occupy active promoters of hematopoietic genes (Gata1, cKit) and rDNA. Unexpectedly, Ddx21 loss does not displace Kdm5a from chromatin but reduces H3K4me3 at these loci, repressing both hematopoietic and ribosomal gene transcription. Although p53 activation drives apoptosis, p53 inhibition only partially rescues hematopoietic failure. Notably, combined pharmacological inhibition of Kdm5a and p53 synergistically restores H3K4me3, protein synthesis, and HSPC colony formation. Our findings reveal a non-canonical function of Ddx21 in epigenetic regulation by counteracting Kdm5a-mediated repression to sustain active transcription. The DDX21-KDM5A complex represents a previously unrecognized chromatin modulator balancing ribosome biogenesis and epigenetic repression, with implications for understanding the pathogenesis of ribosomopathies and developing therapeutic strategies targeting the epigenome-ribosome interface.

title: pH-Responsive Synthetic Cells for Programmable In Situ Protein Synthesis and Release.
abstract: Lipid membrane-bound synthetic cells provide programmable, cell-like compartments for on-demand biomolecule production. However, most cell-free gene expression systems in synthetic cells are regulated by user-imposed cues rather than signals associated with environmental or physiological states. Here, we present an acidity-transducing synthetic cell that converts external pH changes into nucleic acid information to drive in situ protein synthesis. The system integrates gramicidin A proton channels for pH sensing, triplex-forming single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) that releases a trigger ssDNA upon acidification, and a toehold switch RNA that activates translation in response to the released trigger ssDNA. This work further reveals that tuning the annealing length between the pH-responsive and trigger ssDNAs controls the trigger-release pH, which is critical for enabling acid-triggered protein synthesis. The synthetic cells retain their pH-responsive activity when embedded in alginate hydrogels, creating acidity-responsive materials that synthesize proteins in situ rather than release preloaded cargo. Cell-penetrating peptide tagging further enables selective protein release and target-specific binding. This work establishes a molecular transduction strategy for programming synthetic cell materials to sense environmentally relevant acidity and generates functional biomolecules on demand.

title: PEP472, an ncRNA-encoded micropeptide, attenuates oxidative stress-induced senescence and preserves TSPC stemness by stabilizing SIRT1.
abstract: Tendon stem/progenitor cells (TSPCs) play essential roles in tendon homeostasis and repair, but their regenerative capacity is compromised by oxidative stress-induced senescence and the associated loss of stemness. Here, we identified PEP472, a previously uncharacterized micropeptide encoded by a small open reading frame (smORF) within the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) MSTRG.44472.1, as a regulator of TSPC function under oxidative stress. The expression of MSTRG.44472.1 decreased in an H₂O₂-induced TSPC senescence model, and the coding potential of its smORF and translation into PEP472 were subsequently validated. Functional analyses demonstrated that PEP472 attenuated H₂O₂-induced senescence, preserved TSPC stemness, and promoted tenogenic differentiation. Mechanistically, PEP472 increased SIRT1 protein abundance by suppressing proteasome-dependent SIRT1 degradation and enhancing SIRT1 stability. Consistent with a role for SIRT1 in mediating the protective effects of PEP472, pharmacological inhibition of SIRT1 with EX-527 markedly attenuated the anti-senescence effects of PEP472. Together, these findings identify a previously unrecognized MSTRG.44472.1-PEP472-SIRT1 regulatory axis in TSPCs and demonstrate that PEP472 attenuates oxidative stress-induced senescence and preserves TSPC stemness through SIRT1 stabilization. This study highlights PEP472 as a promising micropeptide-based biologic candidate for preventing senescence-associated TSPC dysfunction and supporting tendon regenerative repair.

title: Mitochondrial antiviral signalling protein (MAVS) in cardiovascular diseases (CVD): a novel pharmacological target.
abstract: Mitochondrial antiviral signalling protein (MAVS), also known as interferon-β (IFN-β) promoter stimulator 1 (IPS-1), virus-induced signalling adaptor (VISA), and CARD adaptor inducing IFN-β (CARDIF), has emerged as a regulatory node linking mitochondrial stress, innate immune signalling, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) pathogenesis. In the cardiovascular system, MAVS is activated not only by viral RNA sensors such as retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) and melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5), but also by endogenous danger signals. This activation promotes transcription of NLR family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) and pro-inflammatory cytokines, and facilitates NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and cytokine maturation, processes implicated in myocardial inflammation, remodelling, and dysfunction in conditions such as myocardial hypertrophy, atherosclerosis, and cardiomyopathy. Beyond inflammasome activation, MAVS intersects with multiple cell death and homeostatic pathways relevant to CVD, including apoptosis, autophagy, and, potentially, ferroptosis. Preclinical studies show that genetic ablation of MAVS, or pharmacological interventions that limit mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS), mitochondrial double-stranded RNA (mtdsRNA) release, or downstream innate immune signalling, can attenuate MAVS-associated inflammation, oxidative stress, and metabolic remodelling, thereby slowing disease progression in experimental cardiovascular models. MAVS, however, also performs essential protective functions, particularly in antiviral defence and maintenance of cardiac homeostasis, underscoring the need for context-specific, cell-type-restricted, or pathway-selective modulation rather than indiscriminate inhibition. Collectively, these findings position MAVS as a promising therapeutic target in CVD, warranting further investigation into MAVS-associated signalling pathways and their modulation in cardiovascular contexts.

title: Absolute quantification and profiling of cellular tRNAs by nanopore sequencing and a deep learning classifier.
abstract: Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) link mRNA codons to amino acids during translation. Their abundance and modification states are dynamically regulated and influence translation efficiency, mRNA stability, and proteostasis. Accurate profiling of tRNAs is essential, but deep sequencing suffers from modification-induced biases during cDNA synthesis, while nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) still faces challenges in accurate tRNA profiling. Here, we develop an end-to-end deep learning model, termed nano tRNA classifier, that directly uses nanopore-DRS ionic current signals to classify tRNAs without basecalling. The model achieves 98.2% classification accuracy with high read retention across all Escherichia coli tRNA species. Using an equimolar mixture of native tRNAs as a ground-truth reference, we correct read-count bias, enabling absolute quantification and profiling under diverse culture conditions. We further develop binary classifiers that detect specific tRNA modifications at the single-molecule level with high accuracy. This nanopore-based platform integrates accurate tRNA classification, absolute quantification, and single-molecule modification detection.

title: Interpretable AI-guided discovery of degradable ionizable lipids with enhanced hepatic mRNA delivery in vivo.
abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) enable RNA medicines, yet ionizable-lipid discovery remains largely empirical, particularly when in vitro activity must be translated into functional hepatic delivery in vivo. Here we establish an interpretable discovery framework that combines modular degradable lipid chemistry, high-throughput phenotyping, machine learning, virtual library expansion, and independent in vivo validation to define a learnable ionizable-lipid design space. Starting from a 520-member library, we train an XGBoost model on firefly luciferase (Fluc) expression in HeLa cells and use physicochemical descriptors and molecular fingerprints to prospectively prioritize candidates with higher predicted in vitro transfection activity across a 10,920-member virtual space. In vivo phenotyping subsequently identifies PA97MD101 as a lead ionizable lipid. In mice, PA97MD101 enhances hepatic mRNA expression and Cre-dependent recombination and supports Cas9/sgTtr-mediated TTR suppression. Its performance is associated with pH-dependent membrane activity and reduced lysosomal colocalization. These findings support further evaluation of PA97MD101 for functional hepatic RNA delivery.

title: Engineered CRISPR for nucleic acid imaging at the single-molecule level.
abstract: Accurate and dynamic visualization of nucleic acids at the single-molecule level is essential for elucidating cellular processes, defining disease-associated molecular mechanisms, and advancing molecular diagnostics. Conventional imaging methods often lack the sensitivity, specificity, or spatiotemporal resolution required in complex biological systems. Engineered clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) technologies, leveraging the high programmability of Cas proteins and guide RNAs, have expanded nucleic acid imaging from repetitive and non-repetitive genomic loci to sequence-variant discrimination and individual RNA imaging. This review summarizes major engineering strategies, including Cas protein labeling, guide RNA scaffold modification, and nanomaterial- or protein-assisted signal amplification platforms. We further discuss biomedical applications in live-cell tracking, spatial nucleic acid analysis, and real-time monitoring of cellular dynamics. By examining the biochemical and engineering principles underlying these platforms, we provide a framework for the rational design of CRISPR-based nucleic acid imaging strategies and identify key considerations for overcoming persistent limitations in complex biological environments. Collectively, these advances position engineered CRISPR imaging as a programmable platform for spatially resolved nucleic acid analysis; however, broader application to clinically relevant specimens will require rigorous validation of quantitative robustness and specimen compatibility, together with standardized imaging workflows.

title: mRNA-LNPs encoding Ornithodoros moubata antigens induces humoral and cellular immune responses and tick resistance in rabbits.
abstract: Ornithodoros moubata and Ornithodoros erraticus are important vectors of African swine fever virus and relapsing fever Borrelia spp., highlighting the need for effective and sustainable control strategies. In this study, six previously identified O. moubata vaccine candidates, including salivary and/or midgut antigens cyclophilin (OmCPH), peroxiredoxin (OmPXR), hypothetical protein 275 (OmH275), aquaporin 23 (OmAQP23), subolesin (OmSUB) and Om85, were evaluated as messenger RNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccines. Rabbits received three intradermal immunisations with individual mRNA-LNP formulations, and humoral, cellular, and protective immune responses were assessed. All mRNA-LNP constructs induced antigen-specific IgM and IgG responses and generated antibodies capable of recognising native proteins in tick salivary glands and/or midgut tissues. Antigen stimulation of peripheral blood mononuclear cells revealed antigen-specific cellular responses characterised by increased expression of IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-8, CXCL10, IL-2, and IL-4, although the extent of these responses varied among antigens. OmCPH induced the strongest IL-8 response, OmSUB markedly increased CXCL10, IL-2 and IL-4 expression, and OmH275 elicited consistent IFN-γ and TNF-α responses. Vaccination adversely affected tick feeding, reproduction, development, and survival, with the most pronounced effects observed on female oviposition and fertility. Vaccine efficacies against O. moubata reached 19.8% (OmCPH), 3.7% (OmPXR), 25.6% (OmH275), 10.1% (OmAQP23), 25.2% (OmSUB), and 38.5% (Om85), while efficacies against O. erraticus reached 0%, 26.5%, 6.2%, 11.7%, 10.6%, and 18.5%, respectively. These findings demonstrate that mRNA-LNP vaccination induces both humoral and cellular immune responses against Ornithodoros antigens and provides measurable protection against tick infestations, supporting the application of mRNA technology for the development of multivalent anti-tick vaccines.

title: Nanoscale Immune Activator for Enhancing CD8+ T Cell Infiltration in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: The infiltration of CD8+ T cells into the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) microenvironment is a well-established determinant of immunotherapy efficacy and patient prognosis. However, the regulatory mechanisms governing this process and the therapeutic strategies capable of modulating it remain largely unexplored. Here, we identify HCC-IN-247 as a candidate compound that enhances IFNβ-driven CD8+ T cell infiltration both in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the long noncoding RNA LINC02084 directly interacts with the transcription factor GLIS1 and facilitates its recruitment to the IFNβ promoter. HCC-IN-247 was identified through screening to target the LINC02084-GLIS1 binding interface, thereby stabilizing this RNA-protein complex. Stabilization of the complex significantly enhances IFNβ transcription, which in turn upregulates CXCL10 and CXCL11 expression and promotes CD8+ T cell infiltration. Furthermore, this study engineered a nanoparticle-based delivery system, designated Lip@RA@BSA-PD-L1/IN-247, for the codelivery of HCC-IN-247 and the anti-PD-L1 antibody atezolizumab in HCC treatment. These nanoparticles exhibited robust tumor-specific accumulation and elicited potent synergistic antitumor activity against HCC in mice. Collectively, our findings establish HCC-IN-247 as an activator of the tumor immune microenvironment and provide a preclinical basis for a combined immunotherapeutic approach to HCC.

title: IsoAPA: a multi-species long-read RNA-seq atlas of isoform-resolved alternative polyadenylation.
abstract: Genes are often treated as the primary unit of regulation, yet it is transcript isoforms that ultimately execute regulatory output, shaping mRNA stability, localization, and protein production. Alternative polyadenylation (APA) diversifies these outcomes by generating alternative 3' ends. However, existing resources catalogue polyadenylation sites (PASs) primarily as genomic events, obscuring the transcript isoforms on which individual sites are used. Here, we present IsoAPA (https://isoapa.sls.cuhk.edu.hk), a systematically curated database that leverages PacBio and Oxford Nanopore long-read RNA-seq to resolve PASs while preserving their native isoform context. The current release contains over 2.3 million transcript-resolved PAS records from 816 sample groups across 99 species. IsoAPA reveals widespread PAS multiplicity within fixed transcript backbones, with a mean of 2.52 distinct retained PASs per observed transcript in the union across 286 human sample groups. Transcript-level analysis further uncovers PAS usage patterns that are masked by gene-level aggregation, both in PAS diversity and in context-dependent dominant-site usage. By anchoring each terminal site within its assigned transcript model, IsoAPA reframes APA analysis from a gene-centred description of terminal-site usage to an isoform-resolved view of transcript-end regulation.

title: Whole blood transcriptomics atlas across human diseases.
abstract: We present a WBT Atlas, comprising 4444 WBT samples across 98 distinct health conditions, enabling systematic exploration of disease-associated transcriptomic signatures. Health condition-specific profiles are characterized across immune, metabolic, and cell-type specific features at the gene, gene module, and pathway levels. By integrating matched plasma proteomics data from 1280 participants across 28 health conditions, we further assess blood RNA-protein relationships and demonstrate their complementary biological roles. By integrating RNA and protein signatures, we develop multi-class classification models that accurately distinguish among a wide range of health conditions, with integrated models consistently outperforming those based on single-omics data alone. The identified RNA and protein signatures are validated across ten independent WBT cohorts and the UK Biobank. Together, the WBT Atlas provides a genome-wide resource that enables translational discovery in precision medicine.

title: Protein kinase C is a promising host target for anticoronaviral therapy in vitro and in vivo.
abstract: Host-directed antiviral strategies are urgently needed to counteract emerging SARS-CoV-2 variants. Protein kinase C (PKC) family members are involved in the replication of multiple viruses, but their role in coronavirus infections remains unclear. Building on our previous finding that pan-PKC inhibitors suppress SARS-CoV-2 replication in cultured cells, we herein investigated the underlying mechanism and evaluated the in vivo antiviral efficacy of PKC inhibitors in a mouse hepatitis virus (MHV)-infected mouse model. Go 6983, bisindolylmaleimide I, and sotrastaurin significantly reduced PKCα phosphorylation in Huh7 cells, whereas enzastaurin exhibited only a weak inhibitory effect. Importantly, siRNA-mediated knockdown of PKCα, δ, ε, and ζ substantially impaired SARS-CoV-2 replicon and viral trVLP replication, indicating that multiple PKC isoforms contribute to coronavirus replication. These inhibitors exhibited low cytotoxicity in murine 17Cl-1 cells and reduced MHV-induced cytopathic effects. In BALB/c mice, daily intraperitoneal administration of Go 6983 or bisindolylmaleimide I caused no body weight loss or pulmonary histopathological changes. Prophylactic treatment significantly suppressed lung viral RNA copies by 1-3 orders of magnitude, and alleviated virus-induced inflammation in both the lung and liver. Collectively, our results suggest that multiple PKC isoforms are potential host factors involved in coronavirus replication and PKC inhibitors exert potent antiviral and anti-inflammatory activity in vivo. These findings support the notion that PKC represents a promising host-directed antiviral target against coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2.

title: Hypoxic Stress Induces LARP1-Driven Stress Granules That Protect mRNAs from Decay to Sustain Mitotic Cell Cycle Progression
abstract: Hypoxia is a defining feature of solid tumours that elicits extensive transcriptional and post-transcriptional adaptations. Stress granules (SGs) are frequently observed under hypoxia, yet how they assemble and whether they contribute to hypoxic gene regulation remain poorly understood. Here, we show that hypoxia induces SGs through an assembly mechanism distinct from that of classical acute stresses. Hypoxia SG formation occurs independently of the integrated stress response and instead requires the HIF1-REDD1-mTORCC1-4EBP1 axis. Remarkably, hypoxia SGs assemble despite robust ongoing translation, suggesting that additional mechanisms lower the threshold for RNA condensation. We identify LARP1 as a potential determinant of this process, where it promotes G3BP-dependent SG assembly specifically during hypoxia. Despite their distinct assembly mechanism, hypoxia and arsenite SGs recruit broadly similar RNA populations, with selective differences validated by single-molecule FISH, suggesting that conserved principles govern RNA partitioning across different SG states. Functionally, sequestration into hypoxia SGs correlates with enhance protein expression whereby a subset of mRNAs are protected from decay. Transcriptomic analyses further reveal that this protection sustains a broader gene-expression program enriched for MCM complex and mitotic cell-cycle regulators. Accordingly, disruption of hypoxia SGs reduces mitotic progression and proliferative competence during prolonged hypoxia. Together, our findings establish LARP1-mediated condensation as a mechanism that enables SG assembly despite ongoing translation and reveal that SG sequestration preserves selected mRNAs from decay to sustain the gene-expression programs required for long-term adaptation to hypoxia.

title: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated PD-L1 knockout reshapes temporal transcriptomic responses to PRRSV infection in porcine alveolar macrophages.
abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) suppresses innate antiviral immunity in porcine alveolar macrophages, and the PD-1/PD-L1 axis is thought to contribute to this immune dysregulation. This study investigated how PD-L1 knockout (KO) alters the host transcriptional response to PRRSV infection compared to wild-type (WT) immortalized porcine alveolar macrophages (iPAMs). PD-L1 KO iPAMs were generated by CRISPR/Cas9 targeting exon 2 of porcine CD274 locus, and knockout was confirmed in clone #35. After PRRSV-2 infection, KO#35 cells exhibited approximately 5-fold reduced viral RNA accumulation at 48 h post-infection compared with WT cells. Time-course RNA sequencing at 0, 6, and 48 h post-infection was then performed to characterize the transcriptional consequences of PD-L1 KO during acute PRRSV-2 infection. PD-L1 KO iPAMs exhibited downregulation of immune checkpoint and exhaustion-related genes (LAG3, PDCD1, TIGIT, TOX family) and NF-κB inhibitors (SOCS4, NFKBIA), alongside upregulation of antigen presentation (MHC I/II genes like SLA-2, SLA-5, B2M, SLA-DMA, SLA-DMB, HLA-DRA) and co-stimulatory molecules (CD80, CD86, CD40). Cytokine profiling indicated a reprogrammed response favoring antiviral signaling, including sustained elevation of CXCL10/11, ISGs (MX1/2, ISG15, IFIT1-3), and select interleukins (IL15, IL6), while suppressing pro-inflammatory TNF and CXCL8 across time points. Pathway enrichment analysis revealed significant enrichment of the cytokine-receptor interaction pathway. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) further identified a key co-expression module containing 1,763 DEGs that was associated with innate immune activation. Moreover, protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis detected PXDN as a key hub gene connected to the PI3K-Akt signaling and natural killer cytotoxicity pathways. These findings provide transcriptomic insight into the association between PD-L1 deficiency and altered macrophage transcriptional responses to PRRSV infection in an in-vitro iPAM model and provide a basis for future mechanistic investigation of PD-L1 in PRRSV pathogenesis.

title: Catabolite activator protein and quorum sensing cross-control group behaviors in Vibrio campbellii.
abstract: Vibrio species adapt to different niches by sensing and responding to environmental signals such as nutrients, host cues, and quorum sensing autoinducers. Vibrio campbellii uses the master quorum sensing transcription factor LuxR to control the expression of hundreds of genes at high cell density. Furthermore, many gamma-proteobacteria use the global transcription factor catabolite activator protein (CAP) to control numerous physiologically relevant pathways, many of which are also modulated by quorum sensing, such as competence, biofilm formation, and carbon metabolism. However, the extent to which these two global transcription factors overlap to co-regulate gene expression and bacterial behaviors is understudied. In this work, we used chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled with high-throughput Illumina sequencing (ChIP-seq) and RNA-seq to determine the individual and combined regulons of CAP and LuxR in V. campbellii. We found that CAP and LuxR co-occupied 11 promoters to synergistically or antagonistically co-regulate genes involved with metabolism, respiration, and virulence. It was previously proposed that CAP and LuxR both bound the bioluminescence (luxCDABE) promoter to co-regulate these genes, and our RNA-seq data showed that these were indeed the most strongly co-regulated genes. However, our ChIP-seq data revealed that only LuxR bound the luxCDABE promoter in vivo. This pattern of co-regulation-where both CAP and LuxR strongly impact transcription, but only LuxR binds the promoter-was the most common mechanism observed. Our model for bioluminescence regulation is that CAP indirectly activates luxCDABE expression through the regulation of an intermediate factor. This study established new connections between the global gene regulatory networks underpinning nutrient sensing and population sensing. Vibrio bacteria (vibrios) colonize and infect diverse marine hosts, including corals, fish, oysters, and shrimp, and can also cause life-threatening human infections, all of which are rising annually due to increasing ocean temperatures. To develop effective treatments against Vibrio infections, it is critical to understand the global gene regulation mechanisms vibrios use that enable pathogenic lifestyles. Signal transduction systems in bacteria are well-characterized; however, how vibrios coordinate global gene expression changes in response to multiple environmental inputs is understudied. Here, we determined how the aquaculture pathogen Vibrio campbellii regulates global gene expression in response to bacterial population signals and nutrient availability signals. Our findings help contextualize how vibrios respond to their fluctuating environments in nature.

title: Elevational Adaptation in the Moth Thitarodes xiaojinensis: HSP60A-Mediated Thermal Tolerance Evolution Under Gene Flow.
abstract: Climate warming intensifies thermal selection on high-elevation species, yet the molecular mechanisms enabling rapid adaptation under ongoing gene flow remain poorly understood. We examined differentiation between High-elevation (High) and Low-elevation (Low) ecotype samples of Thitarodes xiaojinensis, an endemic ghost moth of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, using SLAF-seq, RNA-seq profiling and survival experiments. Phylogenetic analyses confirm the two ecotype samples are conspecific, and they differ in forewing phenotype. Population structure at K = 2 uncovers elevation-correlated clustering despite weak genome-wide structure (optimal K = 1). Genome-wide F ST scans (Weir & Cockerham) identify HSP60A as a prominent outlier locus (F ST = 0.391, top 1.4% of genome-wide windows). Targeted PCR amplification and sequencing confirmed a nonsense mutation (Glu378*) in the HSP60A coding sequence. This derived allele was carried by 80% (4/5) of Low individuals and by none of 5 High individuals (0 of 10 chromosome copies, one-sided 95% upper bound on allele frequency ≈ 26%), suggesting that it is associated with incipient ecological divergence between the two ecotypes. Co-expression network analysis grouped the chaperone genes into two systems with divergent thermal responses. The small HSPs were induced 2.3-fold from 8°C to 16°C, whereas the classical chaperones were not induced, and HSP60A was consistently placed within the latter (median biweight midcorrelation +0.56 with classical chaperones versus -0.27 with small HSPs, p = 3.5 × 10-9). Across the three temperatures the Low ecotype expressed HSP60A at lower levels than the High ecotype, significant under log2(TPM + 1) (p = 0.020) but not under the other two scales, and survived better at 16°C (p = 0.0342). These results link a coding variant at HSP60A, its lower transcript level in the Low ecotype and the better survival of that ecotype at 16°C, and identify HSP60A as a candidate locus for ecotype-informed conservation of the Ophiocordyceps sinensis host insect.

title: TLR9 is required in donor blood for inflammation-induced immunization to an alloantigen on transfused RBCs in mice.
abstract: Humoral immunization to alloantigens on transfused red blood cells (RBCs) remains a major barrier to safe and effective blood transfusion in chronically transfused patients. However, only some patients become alloimmunized following multiple transfusion. It was first observed in mice and then confirmed in humans that recipient inflammation at the time of transfusion increases rates of RBC alloimmunization. Viral double-stranded RNA has been extensively studied and shown to enhance alloimmunization through activation of recipient MAVS (mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein) and subsequent induction of alpha-interferon. However, no one has reported testing the role of innate immune receptors on donor cells. Herein, we report that recipient exposure to another innate immune activator (CpG) enhances alloimmunization to transfused RBCs in a TLR9-dependent fashion. In addition, TLR9 is required both on the transfused donor cells and in the recipient. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of innate immune receptors on transfused donor cells regulating RBC alloimmunization. In addition to adding a new conceptual component to the mechanistic landscape of RBC alloimmunization, these findings raise the possibility of decreasing RBC alloimmunization either by selecting RBC units from donors with known hypomorphic TLR9 gene variants or by introducing TLR9 antagonists into donor blood.

title: Development of Cloned B Cell Populations as Immunotherapeutic Agents Against MYC Carcinogenic Proteins.
abstract: The MYC proto-oncogene is one of the most extensively dysregulated transcription factors in cancer, governing cell cycle progression, metabolic adaptation, and immune evasion. Despite its central role in tumor biology, MYC has been considered an undruggable target due to its nuclear localization, lack of enzymatic activity, and involvement in transcriptional regulation. The emergence of B-cell based immunotherapies has reshaped the understanding of tumor immunology, revealing that B cells exert both effector and regulatory roles in tumor microenvironment. The intersection between MYC biology and B-cell function is relevant, as MYC is indispensable for B-cell maturation and is frequently dysregulated in B-cell-derived malignancies such as Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. We focus specifically on the intersection between MYC-driven oncogenic signaling and emerging B-cell-based immunotherapeutic platforms. This review proposes a conceptual reference framework in which MYC is considered not only as a proliferative driver but also as an immune-modulating oncogene that can aid in the design of humoral therapeutic strategies. Therapeutic strategies to inhibit MYC are systematically discussed, including BET and CDK inhibitors, disruption of MYC-MAX dimerization, RNA-based technologies, synthetic lethality approaches, and emerging PROTACs. Cloned B-cell populations, effector B-cells secreting intrabodies, CAR-B platforms, and antibody-based intracellular targeting are areas of focus. An overview is presented of preclinical and clinical advances made thus far, as well as challenges to the successful translation of these therapies for use in patients including tumor heterogeneity, limitations associated with delivery of agents, and risk of inducing autoimmunity. Forecasting the future provides rationale for combining MYC-targeting agents with immunotherapies and using personalized neoantigen-driven B-cell immunotherapies to treat patients with cancer. Overall, these findings support the concept that MYC B-cell-directed strategies will represent a novel means of treating patients with cancer through their development into new classes of therapeutics.

title: A cross-border comparison reveals expanded microbial diversity and zoonotic risk in Rhipicephalus microplus ticks of Yunnan, China.
abstract: Rhipicephalus microplus is a critical vector for numerous agents of livestock and human diseases. Border regions are potential hotspots for pathogen exchange and emerging tick-borne diseases, yet comprehensive surveys of the total pathogen community (virome and microbiome) in ticks from these areas are limited. This study aimed to characterize the microbial diversity within R. microplus across different geographical locations (local vs. imported) and tissue types in Yunnan, China, to understand ecological drivers and assess associated zoonotic risks. We performed meta-transcriptomic sequencing to profile the RNA virome and 16S rRNA gene sequencing to analyze the bacterial microbiome of R. microplus samples. Ticks were dissected into three key tissues: midgut, salivary glands, and ovaries. Bioinformatic and statistical analyses included taxonomic assignment, diversity metrics (alpha and beta diversity), co-occurrence network analysis, and tests for assessing the impact of geographic origin and tissue type on community structure. Our analysis revealed a highly diverse community of virome and bacterial microbiome. The virome comprised 63 viral families, including 28 with known animal hosts, such as the clinically significant families Flaviviridae, Phenuiviridae, and Peribunyaviridae. The bacterial microbiome included 167 bacterial genera, dominated by known pathogenic genera (Coxiella, Rickettsia, Anaplasma, Ehrlichia). We identified three novel viruses. Viral diversity was significantly richer in cross-border than in local samples, and the midgut exhibited the highest viral diversity among tissues. Network analysis indicated potential interactions between specific viral (e.g., Chuviridae) and bacterial taxa. This study reveals that R. microplus in border areas harbors a high diversity of pathogens with zoonotic potential. The composition of this pathogen community is fundamentally shaped by both geographic origin and vector tissue tropism. The elevated diversity at cross-border sites identifies them as key surveillance targets. These findings provide crucial data for informing surveillance strategies and early warning systems against tick-borne diseases in high-risk border regions.

title: Epitranscriptomic regulation in cholangiocarcinoma: mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
abstract: Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) is the second most common primary liver cancer. It is highly invasive, shows early metastasis, and frequently recurs after surgery. These features result in poor clinical outcomes and limited treatment options. Increasing evidence indicates that epigenetic dysregulation plays a key role in the initiation and progression of CCA. Epigenetic modifications include covalent changes to DNA, RNA, and histone proteins. These modifications regulate chromatin structure and gene expression, thereby shaping malignant cellular behavior. Recent studies have shown that epigenetic regulatory networks are widely disrupted in CCA. This disruption leads to both transcriptional and post-transcriptional reprogramming, which promotes tumor growth, invasion, and therapeutic resistance. Among these mechanisms, epitranscriptomic regulation has emerged as an important layer of gene expression control. RNA modifications, such as m6A and other chemical marks, influence RNA stability, splicing, translation, and degradation. These processes contribute to tumor initiation and progression. In this review, we summarize recent advances in epitranscriptomic regulation in CCA. We highlight key regulatory mechanisms and their functional roles in tumor biology. A better understanding of these pathways may provide new biomarkers and therapeutic targets for CCA.

title: Small extracellular vesicle-mediated epithelial-macrophage crosstalk contributes to macrophage dysfunction during PEDV infection.
abstract: Mucosal immune defense depends on coordinated communication between epithelial and immune cells, yet pathogens can disrupt this crosstalk through diverse mechanisms. Here we show that porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV), an enteric alphacoronavirus, reshapes epithelial small extracellular vesicle (sEV) signaling to impair macrophage function. Despite detection by the intestinal innate immune system, PEDV promotes the release of epithelial sEVs enriched in immunoregulatory noncoding RNAs. Among this cargo, miR-190a targets the actin-regulating protein TMOD3 and disrupts F-actin remodeling, reducing macrophage migration. In parallel, the long noncoding RNA TS2083 promotes annexin A2 degradation, impairing phagocytic cup formation and suppressing phagocytosis. Moreover, serum sEVs from PEDV-infected piglets are enriched in both RNAs and impair isolated alveolar macrophage migration and phagocytosis, suggesting distal macrophage modulation. Collectively, these findings implicate sEV-mediated macrophage reprogramming in PEDV-mediated immune evasion and highlight sEV-associated RNAs as potential biomarkers of PEDV infection and therapeutic targets for restoring macrophage-mediated mucosal immunity.

title: The Safety, Pharmacokinetics, and Antiviral Activity of ABI-4334, A Novel Next-Generation Hepatitis B Capsid Assembly Modulator.
abstract: Novel, well-tolerated, short-term therapeutics for chronic hepatitis B virus infection (cHBV) are needed. ABI-4334 is a next-generation capsid assembly modulator that targets the HBV core protein. The safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of ABI-4334 in healthy volunteers and participants with cHBV and antiviral effects in participants with cHBV were examined in two Phase 1 studies. Study 101 was a placebo-controlled study of healthy volunteers that included four single-ascending dose cohorts and two once-daily multiple-ascending dose cohorts randomized 6:2 (ABI-4334:placebo), and one crossover food-effect cohort randomized 3:3 (fed:fasted). Study 102 was a randomized, blinded, placebo-controlled study where participants with cHBV were randomized 8:2 (ABI-4334 [2 dose cohorts]:placebo). Overall, 54 healthy volunteers and 20 participants with cHBV were included in Studies 101 and 102, respectively. Most participants (75%) in Study 102 were hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) negative and generally had lower baseline HBV DNA and pregenomic RNA (pgRNA) levels. ABI-4334 was well tolerated, with no treatment-emergent serious adverse events (AEs) or treatment-emergent AEs leading to study discontinuation. The mean ABI-4334 plasma half-life ranges were comparable across doses in both studies. Following multiple-dose administration in participants with cHBV, the steady-state mean plasma half-life ranged from 17.5 to 27.5 h. HBV DNA declines were observed in both HBeAg-positive (n = 3) and -negative (n = 13) participants across doses. Reductions in pgRNA were observed in participants with detectable pgRNA at baseline. ABI-4334 was well tolerated, with pharmacokinetics and antiviral results supporting the continued development of ABI-4334 as a monotherapy or component of novel combination regimens for cHBV. Trial Registration: Study 101 (NCT05569941). Study 102 (NCT06384131).

title: Manganese Dioxide Nanozyme-Integrated Aligned Nanofibers Promote Diabetic Wound Repair through Growth Arrest-Specific Protein 6-Mediated Fibroblast-to-Macrophage Communication.
abstract: Chronic diabetic wounds remain difficult to treat because excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS), persistent inflammation, and impaired neovascularization collectively hinder tissue repair. Here, we present a bioinspired aligned electrospun nanofiber membrane composed of methacrylated gelatin and o-nitrobenzyl-modified gelatin and functionalized with manganese dioxide (MnO2) nanozymes to regulate the wound microenvironment. Upon hydration and brief ultraviolet irradiation, the membrane forms a conformable nanofibrous hydrogel that closely adapts to irregular wound beds. Among three MnO2 loadings, the formulation containing 180 μg/mL MnO2 was selected as the optimized formulation because it attenuated intracellular ROS while promoting fibroblast proliferation and migration and endothelial angiogenic activity. Mechanistic studies showed that the optimized hydrogel promoted fibroblast secretion of growth arrest-specific protein 6 (Gas6), which attenuated inflammatory macrophage responses and enhanced reparative macrophage responses. Gas6 knockdown weakened these effects, whereas recombinant Gas6 recapitulated them. Single-cell RNA sequencing identified treatment-associated changes in wound cell states and suggested Gas6-associated fibroblast-macrophage communication through computational ligand-receptor analysis. In streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice, the optimized hydrogel accelerated wound closure and enhanced vascularization, re-epithelialization, and collagen remodeling. These findings establish an aligned nanozyme-functionalized nanofibrous hydrogel that links redox regulation to Gas6-associated fibroblast-to-macrophage signaling for diabetic wound repair.

title: The mechanism of METTL6/DALRD3 regulating cell cycle-mediated chemoresistance in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Chemoresistance worsens the prognosis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). This study focuses on how methyltransferase-like protein 6 (METTL6)/DALR anticodon binding domain containing 3 (DALRD3) regulates cell cycle progression and impacts HCC chemoresistance. HCC cell lines with relatively low or high METTL6 expression were intervened with cisplatin (DDP) to construct DDP-resistant cell models, and later transfected with overexpression (oe)-METTL6 plasmid, oe-DALRD3 plasmid, small interfering RNA (si)-METTL6, and/or si-DALRD3. A battery of cellular biological functional experiments and DDP drug sensitivity tests were performed to characterize the modulatory effects of METTL6 or DALRD3 on HCC chemoresistance. The interaction between METTL6 and DALRD3 was validated using coimmunoprecipitation. 3-methylcytosine (m3C) modification and expression were further detected using dot blot and Northern blot assays. A subcutaneous xenograft mouse model was established with METTL6- or DALRD3-deficient HCC cells, which were exposed to DDP for experimental validation of in vitro findings. METTL6 and DALRD3 were upregulated in DDP-resistant HCC cells, and their upregulation in HCC tissues correlated with poor prognosis. Re-expression of METTL6 or DALRD3 led to strengthened cell proliferation, aggravated cell cycle progression, and augmented DDP chemoresistance. The validated METTL6-DALRD3 interaction increased m3C modification. Northern blot further validated serine transfer RNA-m3C at position 32 (tRNASer-m3C32) modification mediated by the METTL6-DALRD3 complex. Rescue experiments unveiled that DALRD3 overexpression reversed METTL6 knockdown-mediated HCC phenotypes. Either METTL6 or DALRD3 knockdown potentiated DDP chemosensitivity in HCC xenograft mice. METTL6/DALRD3 mediated tRNASer-m3C32 modification may participate in DDP resistance in HCC cells by regulating cell cycle progression.

title: iCellOmics: connecting multi-omics profiles and phenotype evidence across industrially relevant cell lines.
abstract: Industrially relevant cell lines include direct production hosts for biologics, vaccines, and viral vectors, as well as biomedical models that serve as references for host-cell engineering and comparative studies. However, their genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic profiles, together with literature-derived phenotype information, remain distributed across different repositories, project outputs, and publications. Here, we present iCellOmics (https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/icellomics), an open-access database that integrates multi-omics data for industrially relevant cell lines within a unified data and analysis framework. The current release covers 17 cell lines and provides reference genomes for seven species, encompassing 144 018 protein-coding genes, 170 408 888 genomic variants, 673 differential-expression comparisons, 30 distinct single-cell RNA-seq BioProjects comprising 1 047 274 cells, 287 089 415 ATAC-seq peaks, 37 213 deduplicated literature-curated gene-phenotype relationships spanning 104 standardized phenotype subcategories. The database supports both cell line-centric browsing of available datasets and gene-centric exploration of cross-omics analysis results. Additionally, iCellOmics offers online GO and KEGG enrichment analysis tools to facilitate further data exploration. In summary, iCellOmics provides a valuable starting point for investigating gene-phenotype relationships in industrially relevant cell lines and supports cell-line engineering and the development of improved producer lines.

title: Identification and Biological Evaluation of Fisetin as a Novel DYRK1B Inhibitor in Ovarian Cancer with Apoptotic and Ferroptotic Effects.
abstract: DYRK1B kinase has emerged as an important regulator of tumor survival, quiescence, and chemotherapy resistance, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Natural compounds are well-known for their anticancer properties and are being studied extensively for their ability to modulate cancer-related signaling pathways. This study aimed to screen and identify a natural compound that functions as a DYRK1B inhibitor and evaluate its potential as a therapeutic candidate for ovarian cancer treatment. We used virtual screening, in-silico molecular docking and in-vitro kinase assay to identify fisetin as a potential DYRK1B inhibitor exhibiting an IC50 of 1.2 μM. Subsequent validation through in-vitro analysis on ovarian cancer cell lines revealed a reduced phosphorylation of DYRK1B downstream targets, characterized by decreased p27 phosphorylation at (Ser 10) and increased cyclin D1 expression, indicating cell cycle re-entry of quiescent cells following effective inhibition of DYRK1B. This inhibition further triggered DNA damage and apoptosis by the accumulation of γ-H2AX, followed by the cleavage of caspase 3 and PARP. To further investigate the mechanistic role of fisetin, RNA-seq was performed, which showed an enrichment of the ferroptosis pathway. The validation of ferroptosis-associated RNA-seq data using qPCR and Western blot analysis confirmed the upregulation of transferrin receptor (TFRC) and downregulation of the iron exporter SLC40A1, leading to iron accumulation. In addition, GPX4, a crucial protein that inhibits ferroptosis by preventing lipid peroxidation, was also found to be decreased. Lipid Peroxidation assay by C11-BODIPY confirmed an increase in lipid ROS, which was effectively reversed by the treatment with ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin-1. In summary, our results revealed that fisetin is an effective DYRK1B inhibitor that further induces ovarian cancer cell death via apoptosis and also modulates ferroptosis associated pathways, underscoring the therapeutic potential of fisetin in ovarian cancer treatment.

title: ACKR3 Upregulation Under Hyperglycemia Associates with Endothelial Dysfunction.
abstract: Diabetes is a metabolic disorder characterized by chronic hyperglycemia and is associated with cardiovascular complications. Endothelial cell dysfunction is a common feature of both diabetes and its vascular complications. In this study, RNA-seq data from aortic specimens of diabetic patients were analyzed to identify candidate genes that are potentially involved in regulating endothelial cell function under hyperglycemic conditions. Among the identified GPCRs, ACKR3 was singled out as a promising candidate. Expression of ACKR3 in the vessels of diabetic animals and the HUVEC cell line under hyperglycemia conditions was assessed. Subsequently, the function of the ACKR3 gene was investigated by downregulation of ACKR3 at hyperglycemic conditions in the HUVEC cell line. Our data showed that expression of Ackr3 in the vessels of diabetic animals was increased. Furthermore, treatment of HUVECs under hyperglycemic conditions (25 mM D-glucose) for 24 h and 48 h resulted in elevated ACKR3 expression at both mRNA and protein levels. Functional analyses revealed that ACKR3 downregulation resulted in significant reductions in oxidative stress levels, inflammation, and the rate of endothelial cell apoptosis under hyperglycemic conditions. Additionally, ACKR3 downregulation reduced the expression of adhesion molecules (ICAM and VCAM), leading to decreased monocyte adhesion under hyperglycemic conditions. Our findings suggest that hyperglycemia-induced ACKR3 up-regulation may contribute to endothelial cell dysfunction in diabetic vessels. Therefore, targeting ACKR3 could offer valuable insights for developing therapeutic strategies against diabetes-related vascular complications.

title: Reducing reactive lipids improves cardiac metabolic and diastolic function in pulmonary hypertension models.
abstract: Reactive oxygen species are increased across most pulmonary hypertension (PH) etiologies, resulting in increased reactive lipid dicarbonyls, which form protein adducts and impair mitochondrial function. We hypothesized that reducing reactive lipids would reduce right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) and improve cardiac function by eliminating protein-lipid damage feedback loops. We used 2-hydroxybenzylamine (2-HOBA) to scavenge reactive lipids in three complimentary mouse models of PH: AKR-high fat diet (HFD, metabolic stress), LNAME-HFD (cardiometabolic syndrome), and pulmonary artery banding (PAB, load stress). Cardiac function was measured by echocardiography and catheterization. RV energy metabolism was determined by oxygraphy. Mass spectrometry analyzed lipids and ceramides; O-link and RNA-Seq evaluated proteomic and gene expression in lungs, RV, and LV. Reducing reactive lipids with 2-HOBA resulted in a ~ 10% reduction in RVSP, reduced diastolic dysfunction, reduced plasma lipids and ceramides, and normalized RV fatty acid oxidation that was severely impaired in the AKR-HFD and PAB models. Proteomic and RNA changes in the lungs, RV, and LV suggested reduced oxidative damage and inflammatory signaling and altered developmental and actin organization signaling; these changes are plausibly associated with the improved adaptation. Some changes were sex specific, including a 4x higher cardiac fatty acid content in males than females. Reactive lipid scavenging improves cardiac metabolic and diastolic function and right ventricular systolic pressure through restoration of mitochondrial function and reduced oxidative protein damage. The magnitude of hemodynamic improvement combined with substantial diastolic function improvement suggests clinical potential, particularly for PH patients with metabolic comorbidities.

title: The landscape of cell surface target expression in treatment resistant early-stage breast cancer.
abstract: Disease recurrence after definitive therapy remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality in early-stage breast cancer, with limited options for treatment intensification. Cell surface-targeted (CST) therapies, including antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), radiopharmaceuticals, and immune-based approaches, have demonstrated success in treating malignancies. However, the known CST repertoire in breast cancer is narrow, largely restricted to HER2 and TROP2, highlighting an unmet need for novel targets in treatment-resistant disease. We profiled CST expression using large-scale gene expression datasets annotated with clinical outcomes, including SCAN-B (n ≈ 10,000), aggregated neoadjuvant chemotherapy cohorts (n ≈ 4,000), and the randomized SWEBCG91RT trial (n = 765). CSTs with therapies in clinical trials were prioritized. RNA-protein correlation was assessed using CPTAC and SCMP datasets. Associations with recurrence-free survival (RFS) and treatment response were analyzed using Cox regression and Fisher's exact test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Of 78 CSTs under active clinical investigation, RNA expression strongly predicted protein expression (median accuracy 80-94%). In ER+ breast cancer treated with endocrine therapy, nine CSTs (including CEACAM5/6, EPCAM, NECTIN4) were associated with significantly worse RFS. Of these, EPCAM and CEACAM5 were also associated with poor outcomes specifically after radiotherapy in the SWEBCG91RT trial. In HER2 + disease, high expression of FOLH1 and TNFRSF10B predicted relapse despite anti-HER2 therapy. In triple-negative breast cancer, six CSTs were associated with residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy. These analyses identify potential candidates for repositioning CST drugs, and single-cell analysis revealed substantial intratumoral heterogeneity for several targets, informing payload selection strategies. CSTs associated with treatment resistance across breast cancer subtypes represent actionable opportunities for therapeutic repositioning. These findings provide a framework for rational integration of CST therapies in early-stage breast cancer.

title: GAS5 in Colorectal Cancer: A Multifaceted Long Non-Coding RNA in Tumor Suppression, Prognosis and Therapeutic Targeting.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most prevalent cancers worldwide, particularly affecting developed countries. Many pathways and mechanisms have been implicated in the development of CRC, and one of the targets of interest is the long non-coding ribonucleic acid (lncRNA), growth arrest specific 5 (GAS5). GAS5 has been observed to play an important role in many other cancers, and CRC is not an exception. This paper aims to understand the role and mechanisms played by GAS5 in relation to CRC progression. GAS5 has a complex role, with one of its major functions being its competitive endogenous nature that can downregulate multiple microRNAs such as miR-485-5p, miR-137, miR-26b, miR-21, miR-34a, miR-182-5p, miR-128-3p, and miR-221, which have implications in tumour growth and suppression. It is also observed to interact with proteins directly, such as the Yes-Associated Protein (YAP). Both clinical and laboratory evidence support the fact that in the context of CRC, GAS5 overexpression is a protective factor, while its underexpression is related to poorer prognosis and reduced survival. This has opened up its potential as a prognostic biomarker, as well as a therapeutic target to treat multiple cancers, including CRC. However, more research is still required to address existing knowledge gaps. In conclusion, GAS5 plays multiple roles and is an important player in cancer regulation, including CRC, and it holds good potential to be a biomarker and a therapeutic target.

title: SCAN-seq2 reveals mitochondrial metabolic alterations and proteostasis-related transcriptional signatures during human oocyte aging.
abstract: Ovarian aging, characterized by declines in both oocyte quantity and quality, represents a major challenge to female reproductive health. However, the age-associated transcriptional alterations underlying human oocyte aging remain incompletely understood. Differential expression analysis between young and aged oocytes identified 63 age-associated differentially expressed genes, including increased expression of ribosome-associated genes, oxidative-phosphorylation-related genes such as COX5B and UQCRC2, the ubiquitin-associated gene UBA52, and mtDNA-encoded OXPHOS transcripts including MT-ND4 and MT-ND4L, together with reduced expression of the antioxidant-response gene GSTA1 and the mitochondrial respiratory-chain gene NDUFA9. Functional enrichment analyses revealed biological processes related mainly to translation, protein targeting, ribosomal functions, and oxidative phosphorylation. Further subcluster analysis identified an aged-enriched oocyte population with broader mitochondrial-related transcriptional alterations and enrichment of DNA-damage-response pathways. Subsequent PPI analysis of the intersecting genes identified two exploratory functional modules related to mitochondrial respiratory-chain processes and ribosome/ubiquitin-associated proteostasis. These findings highlight age-associated transcriptional signatures in human oocytes involving mitochondrial metabolism and proteostasis-associated processes, and reveal molecular heterogeneity among aged oocyte populations. Together, these results provide insights into the molecular changes associated with human oocyte aging and establish a transcriptomic framework for future studies of reproductive aging.

title: Salidroside regulates blood-brain barrier integrity via Lcn2-NLRP3 signaling axis inhibition for high-altitude hypoxic brain injury intervention.
abstract: High-altitude hypoxic brain injury (HHBI) is a central nervous system injury disease induced by high-altitude hypobaric and hypoxic environment, which disrupts normal cerebral metabolism and neurological function and triggers multi-dimensional pathological damage in brain tissues. Among these pathological events, blood-brain barrier (BBB) injury represents a critical initiating and aggravating facet of HHBI, which drives subsequent cerebral inflammation, cerebral edema and progressive brain tissue deterioration. Current clinically commonly used drugs can only relieve partial discomforts caused by high-altitude hypoxia, and fail to achieve precise prevention and treatment of HHBI as well as favorable safety profile prognosis. Salidroside (Sal), the core active ingredient of the classic Tibetan medicine Rhodiola crenulata, exerts prominent anti-hypoxia and neuroprotective effects, yet its specific molecular regulatory mechanisms remain poorly elucidated. Combining in vivo and in vitro experiments, this study aimed to explore the novel mechanism by which Sal alleviates BBB injury and thereby prevents and treats HHBI via regulating the Lcn2-NLRP3 signaling axis. After acclimatization, mice were randomly assigned to control, model, dexamethasone (0.5 mg/kg), and Sal (50 and 100 mg/kg) groups, followed by 7-day consecutive administration of corresponding drugs. A low-pressure oxygen chamber was used to simulate high-altitude environments to establish the mouse HHBI model. The WBP respiratory detection system and Morris water maze test were employed to assess alterations in respiratory function and memory cognitive capacity of HHBI mice. A hematology analyzer and H&E staining were utilized to characterize systemic and cerebral inflammatory injury, whereas evans blue staining and brain water content measurement were performed to evaluate hypoxic impacts on BBB permeability. Super-resolution imaging (NIR-Ⅱ imaging and TEM) was adopted to detect cerebral microvascular blood circulation and ultrastructural alterations. Subsequently, RNA-seq was conducted to screen potential molecular targets mediating Sal conferred therapeutic effects against HHBI. Moreover, molecular docking, DFT calculation, alanine scanning and LSPR analysis were implemented to simulate the binding potential and stability between Sal and proteins of the Lcn2-NLRP3 signaling axis, and protein-protein docking and Co-IP further verified the potential binding and regulatory interaction between Lcn2 and NLRP3. Western blot and multiplex immunofluorescence staining were used to demonstrate the molecular mechanism by which Sal alleviates hypoxic BBB injury via modulating the Lcn2-NLRP3 signaling axis. In vitro, a CoCl₂ induced hypoxic model was established in bEnd.3 cells. CCK-8 assay, EdU staining and LDH release assay were used to evaluate the effects of Sal on proliferative activity of hypoxic bEnd.3 cells. DCFH-DA and JC-1 staining were applied to detect intracellular ROS levels and mitochondrial membrane potential. Label-free cellular imaging enabled continuous monitoring of mitochondrial morphological changes under hypoxia, and TEM further observed mitochondrial ultrastructural damage. Mitochondrial superoxide, mPTP and mtDNA staining together with SOD, MDA, GSH-PX and ATP quantification were performed to analyze hypoxia and Sal mediated changes in mitochondrial function. Furthermore, cell scratch wound healing, tube-formation and cell migration assays examined hypoxic vascular functional changes, while TEER resistance and FITC-dextran permeability assays assessed paracellular permeability. Western blot combined with multiplex flow cytometry was used to analyze Sal regulated expression of Lcn2, NLRP3 and downstream inflammatory factors. In addition, the Lcn2 inhibitor ZINC00640089 and target specific siRNA were employed to validate the regulatory role of Lcn2 on NLRP3. Finally, CETSA was further performed to determine the binding stability of Sal to Lcn2-NLRP3 signaling axis proteins. The results demonstrated that Sal exerted robust anti-hypoxic neuroprotective effects in HHBI mice by alleviating cerebral hypoxic stress, suppressing neuroinflammation, improving cerebral microcirculation, maintaining BBB integrity, and upregulating TJ proteins. In vivo data indicated that Sal intervention markedly improved basal respiratory function and alleviated cerebral memory and cognitive impairment in HHBI mice. Meanwhile, Sal effectively mitigated cerebral inflammatory injury induced by acute hypoxic stimulation and restored excessive BBB hyperpermeability. Mechanistically, acute endothelial inflammation and TJ disruption serve as key drivers of HHBI progression, which is predominantly modulated by aberrant activation of the Lcn2-NLRP3 signaling axis. Combined molecular docking, DFT calculation, LSPR detection and alanine scanning analyses confirmed the high-affinity and stable binding of Sal to core proteins of the Lcn2-NLRP3 axis. Western blot and immunofluorescence staining further revealed that Sal effectively alleviated BBB damage by negatively regulating the Lcn2-NLRP3 signaling cascade, and verified the favorable colocalization of Lcn2 with cerebral vascular endothelium. In vitro experiments showed that Sal markedly reversed hypoxia-triggered mitochondrial dysfunction, as evidenced by reduced mitochondrial superoxide accumulation, inhibited mPTP opening and mtDNA leakage, as well as restored MMP, ATP synthesis, and balanced levels of SOD, MDA and GSH-PX, thereby suppressing apoptosis in hypoxic bEnd.3 cells. Furthermore, Sal stabilized endothelial vascular structure and barrier function, increased transepithelial electrical resistance and elevated TJ protein expression in hypoxic endothelial cells. Multiplex flow cytometry further validated the regulatory effect of Sal on hypoxic inflammatory responses. Moreover, intervention with the Lcn2 inhibitor ZINC00640089 and Lcn2-specific siRNA further confirmed that Lcn2 acts as an indispensable upstream regulator of NLRP3 inflammasome activation and subsequent inflammatory cascades. Collectively, this study demonstrated that Sal ameliorates acute hypoxia‑induced mitochondrial dysfunction, thereby inhibiting excessive Lcn2 accumulation, suppressing subsequent NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activation, and blocking downstream inflammatory cascade amplification. These effects ultimately alleviate vascular structural and functional damage, thereby exerting prominent preventive and therapeutic effects against HHBI.

title: TIPIN Couples Epigenetic Rewiring to EGFR Stabilization and Lenvatinib Resistance in Liver Cancer.
abstract: Liver cancer is an aggressive tumor marked by substantial morbidity and mortality. Timeless-interacting protein (TIPIN) is dysregulated in multiple cancers, but its epigenetic regulation, biological function, and downstream pathways in liver cancer remain poorly defined. This study sought to explore TIPIN's function in liver cancer tumorigenesis, metastasis, and lenvatinib resistance. We analyzed TCGA data and 94 paired clinical samples.
